text: You've spent thirteen courses learning the ServiceNow platform, but most of those lessons weren't portfolio pieces — they were concept-building. Only a handful of labs and capstones actually produced a finished artifact you can point to. This lesson walks through the six that are genuinely worth showcasing, and the honest way to describe each one.

Six candidates stand out. The Flow Designer automation build from course 4, a multi-step flow with triggers and approvals. The scoped application from courses 5 and 6, with real Business Rules and Script Includes — actual server-side logic. The REST integration from course 7, built with IntegrationHub. The ITSM implementation configuration from course 8. The CMDB and CSDM data model from course 9. And the Technical Architecture capstone from course 13 — the Meridian Health Network enterprise architecture exercise, with a real instance-strategy decision and an Architecture Decision Record.

Here's the part worth getting right: every one of these was built on a free Personal Developer Instance, as a course lab or capstone. None of them went live for real end users, none carried real production data, none survived real change-advisory-board politics. That doesn't make the work worthless — building a working scoped application is genuinely harder than describing one in the abstract. But describe it honestly: a self-directed project built to demonstrate applied skill, not a production system you shipped to a client. The honest version holds up better once someone starts asking follow-up questions.

Different roles want to hear about different work first. For an Administrator conversation, lead with the ITSM configuration and the Flow Designer build. For a Developer conversation, lead with the scoped application and the REST integration — real code, a real integration pattern. For anything touching Implementation Specialist or Technical Architect territory, lead with the CMDB/CSDM model and the Meridian Health Network capstone.
Six real artifacts, honestly described, matched to the right conversation. Next up: turning that same material into language that actually gets a resume read.
